title: Learning Lesson 7: Bad Learning Strategies Are Popular
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This installment of the Learning Lesson series presents Stephen Chew's second learning "pitfall": that students tend to prefer the least effective study strategies for long-term learning. Stuart names the three most common offenders — mindlessly rereading text, mindlessly highlighting, and passively "going over" notes — and identifies what they share: all three are passive and low-effort, which is exactly why they're popular despite not working. He explains the underlying trap in accessible terms: passive review builds a feeling of familiarity that gets mistaken for actual learning, when in reality the student has only memorized what the notes or highlighted text look like, not the material itself. In place of these strategies, Stuart lists what cognitive science shows does work — creating meaning, chunking information, elaborating and connecting new material to prior knowledge, and practicing retrieval — framing all of them as more effortful, "aggressive" alternatives to passive review.
points: The three most popular study strategies — rereading, highlighting, and passively reviewing notes — are popular precisely because they're passive and low-effort, not because they work.
Stuart's core diagnosis is that passive review produces familiarity with what the material looks like, which students mistake for actually knowing the material.
The fix requires substituting effortful, "aggressive" strategies for passive ones: creating meaning, chunking, elaborating with connections to prior knowledge, and practicing active recall.
He explicitly ties the chunking strategy back to the working-memory bottleneck from earlier in the series, showing how the pitfalls and bottlenecks interlock rather than standing as separate lessons.
quotes: Students often prefer the least effective study strategies for long-term learning. Let's get it down, and then let's talk about strategies that work and strategies that don't.
Now notice a commonality between the three of these: all of them are kind of passive. Remember how fired up I got yesterday talking about being aggressive? That's the opposite of passive.
The trouble, of course, is that being familiar with your notes doesn't mean that you've learned the course material. You've just built some vague pictures in your mind of what the notes look like.
The solutions, then are to basically get AGGRESSIVE with understanding what the heck you're supposed to learn and getting that information organized in your mind.

As you're studying, focus on creating meaning — on understanding what you're trying to learn about. Organize information into meaningful chunks. Elaborate on the information you're learning — try to make connections between it and other things you know.
